name: Yantai
title: Ultrasonic Thickness Gauging Yantai | Bulkers, Ro-ro & Ferries
description: Ship thickness measurement in Yantai: hold, car deck, hatch cover and ballast tank gauging on bauxite Capesizes, car carriers, ro-pax ferries and tankers.
h1: Ship UTM and Hull Thickness Gauging in Yantai, Shandong
intro: Yantai, on the northern coast of the Shandong Peninsula where the Yellow Sea meets the Bohai Strait, is one of China's main import gateways for bauxite and a growing export base for vehicles. Capesize bulk carriers arriving from West Africa, car carriers loading for overseas markets and the ro-pax ferries that cross to Dalian all work here. Long bulk discharges and ferry stand-downs leave room for gauging. Every Yantai job is staffed by technicians who fly in from India for that ship, timed to the agent's berth plan.

highlights.p: Yantai handles a very large share of China's bauxite imports, much of it from West Africa, so big bulk carriers spend days alongside discharging. Once holds are swept, tank tops, hopper plating and frames can be gauged before the long ballast voyage back to the loading port.

Yantai's ro-ro services load commercial vehicles and cars for overseas markets. While a pure car and truck carrier loads level by level or waits for cargo, empty decks, ramps and hoistable deck panels can be measured without upsetting the stowage plan.

highlights.h: A shipbuilding town as well as a port
highlights.p: Yantai CIMC Raffles builds large ro-pax ferries and freight ro-ros for the Bohai Strait operators, so new ships are delivered from yards in the city. Owners can record baseline thickness readings on a young ship while it is still close to its builder.

port.h: Yantai: bauxite, vehicles and the Bohai Strait crossing
p: Yantai faces north across the water towards the Liaodong Peninsula, at the point where the Bohai Strait opens into the Yellow Sea. The port is part of Shandong Port Group, alongside Qingdao and Rizhao, and spreads along the coast in several areas: the older harbour at Zhifu Bay beside the city centre, the newer deep-water west port, and further west the Longkou port area facing into the Bohai. Ships approach through open water with no locks or river passage, but the north coast takes strong northerly winds in winter, and swell can make launch transfers at the outer anchorages difficult. Sea fog is common in spring and early summer, and in that season visibility rather than wind tends to decide whether anchorage work goes ahead.

Bulk cargo dominates the tonnage. Yantai has become one of China's principal bauxite import ports, feeding alumina refineries inland by rail and road, and the bauxite arrives mainly from West Africa in Capesize bulk carriers. Alongside it the port handles coal, ore, grain, fertiliser and general cargo, crude and products at its liquid terminals, and containers on intra-Asia services. Vehicle exports have grown into a trade of their own, with ro-ro services linking Yantai to dozens of countries and new LNG-fuelled car carriers making their maiden departures here. Each trade brings ships in a different condition: hard-worked bulk carriers, tankers with vetting deadlines, and modern ro-ro ships whose decks and ramps carry wheeled traffic on every voyage. A superintendent planning a Yantai job therefore starts from the trade the ship is in, because that decides which spaces will be free and for how long.

Passenger and freight traffic across the Bohai Strait is the third strand. Ro-pax ferries and freight ro-ros run between Yantai and Dalian, and the main ferry operator on the route has its home in Yantai, so its ships return here between rotations and for planned maintenance. The city also builds ships: Yantai CIMC Raffles, which spent many years building offshore drilling units, now also builds large ro-pax ferries and freight ro-ros for the Bohai operators. Heavy docking of ocean-going bulk carriers and tankers, by contrast, normally happens at yards in Dalian, Qingdao or the Yangtze delta, so thickness readings taken in Yantai are often the pre-docking record that travels on with the ship. Without a large repair yard of its own for that tonnage, the port's value to an owner lies in its long cargo stays.

facilities.h: Where gauging takes place in Yantai
p: At the bulk berths, the window opens as discharge progresses. Bauxite is grabbed out hold by hold, and once a hold is empty and swept the tank top, hopper slopes, lower stool and frame brackets can be measured while the remaining holds are still working. Ballast tanks follow when the ship takes on ballast for departure and the chief officer can release tanks for ventilation and entry. At the ro-ro berths, the decks themselves are the work site: measurement runs on the levels that are empty, with the deck crew moving the team ahead of the loading gangs. Tankers at the liquid berths offer deck plating, piping and certified ballast spaces under the terminal's permit system.

Ferries are measured at their home berths during scheduled stand-downs or overnight lay-overs, and new ships can be gauged before delivery or at their first docking while still close to the builder. Anchorage work in the approaches is possible for ships waiting for a bulk berth, using a launch arranged by the agent, but winter gales and spring fog limit the days it can be done. Where a ship needs docking for steel renewal, the data measured in Yantai goes to the chosen yard in Dalian, Qingdao or further south, so the plate order can be placed before the ship arrives.
list: Bulk berths in the west port — hold and ballast tank gauging on Capesize and Panamax bulk carriers after bauxite or coal discharge.
Longkou port area — bulk carriers on the Bohai side of the peninsula; hold, hatch cover and coaming readings during discharge.
Ro-ro berths — car deck, ramp and hoistable deck gauging on car and truck carriers loading vehicles for export.
Ferry berths — car deck, ballast tank and shell readings on Bohai Strait ro-pax ships during planned stand-downs.
Liquid berths — deck, piping and certified ballast space gauging on product and chemical tankers within terminal rules.
Anchorages in the Yantai approaches — ballast-condition gauging for buyers or pre-docking estimates, weather permitting.

context.h: Port state control, cargo rules and Yantai's trades
p: The China Maritime Safety Administration carries out port state control at Yantai under the Tokyo MoU, and its officers see a steady stream of bulk carriers from the long West African trade. Ships that load bauxite in tropical rain and then make long ocean passages need sound hatch covers, coamings and hold structure, and wasted or distorted coaming plating is a common reason for questions at the gangway. The IMSBC Code now treats some bauxite fines as a cargo that may liquefy, which has made the condition of hold structure and hatch covers a closer concern for charterers and P&I clubs on this trade than it was a decade ago.

The Bohai ferries and coastal ships answer to a different regime: ships that never leave Chinese waters are surveyed by their flag administration and class rather than by port state control, yet daily crossings wear car deck plating, ramp hinges and ballast tanks quickly all the same. For scrubber-fitted bulk carriers and car carriers, China's domestic rules restrict open-loop wash-water discharge in port waters and some coastal areas, so the exhaust gas cleaning system is often idle while the ship lies at Yantai, which makes that a practical time to inspect its piping. Operators should confirm the current rules for Bohai waters before arrival.

jobs.h: Typical ship inspection jobs at Yantai
jobs.p: Yantai work is shaped by long bulk discharges, ro-ro loading and the ferries' fixed timetable. Superintendents of bauxite carriers ask for hold and ballast tank readings after discharge, ahead of a renewal survey or to follow known wastage; car carrier operators want decks and ramps checked between voyages; and ferry owners book gauging into their maintenance stand-downs. Buyers looking at bulk carriers on the West African trade sometimes use a Yantai discharge for a pre-purchase inspection. Each programme is scoped against the ship's previous thickness report so that new readings land on the same points and corrosion rates between surveys can be worked out.
list: Hold and topside tank gauging on a Capesize after bauxite discharge, following up substantial corrosion recorded at the last intermediate survey.
Hatch cover and coaming thickness measurement on a bulk carrier before it returns to load bauxite in the West African rainy season.
Car deck, ramp and hoistable deck gauging on a pure car and truck carrier during its loading call, with crack checks at ramp hinges.
Ballast tank and car deck readings on a Bohai Strait ro-pax ferry during a planned stand-down, ahead of its docking survey.
Pre-purchase condition gauging of a Panamax bulk carrier at anchor in the Yantai approaches for a prospective buyer.
Baseline gauging of a newly built ferry before its first docking, so later surveys have a reference set to compare against.

logistics: Yantai Penglai International Airport, west of the city, handles domestic flights and some international routes, and most teams connect through a Chinese hub such as Beijing or Shanghai. The ship's agent arranges port passes for the bulk, liquid and ro-ro terminals and books a launch for any anchorage boarding. Each technician from India needs a Chinese business visa, normally applied for with an invitation letter from a company in China, and some terminals want personnel details in advance for access, so we start once the berth or stand-down date is known.

faqs.q: Can you gauge a bauxite carrier's holds during discharge at Yantai?
faqs.a: Yes. Bauxite discharge takes several days on a Capesize, and holds are emptied in sequence. Once a hold is swept and released by the chief officer, we measure tank top, hopper slopes, stools and frames, concentrating on areas with grab damage or a corrosion history. Ballast tanks are usually gauged nearer departure, when the ship is ballasting and tanks can be ventilated and certified.

faqs.q: Is anchorage gauging possible off Yantai in winter?
faqs.a: Sometimes, but it should not be relied on. Northerly gales in the winter months can make launch transfers unsafe for days at a time, and spring fog can do the same. For a ship waiting off Yantai we keep a short list of priority spaces and plan to complete the rest at the berth, where discharge gives a more dependable window.

faqs.q: Can car deck plating be measured while vehicles are being loaded?
faqs.a: Yes, on the decks that are not being worked. We coordinate with the chief officer and the stevedores so the team measures empty levels ahead of or behind the loading, and keeps off ramps while cargo is moving. Car deck plating, deck girders, ramp plating and hinge areas are the usual targets, with magnetic particle testing at hinge and support welds where cracking is suspected.

faqs.q: Where do ships that call at Yantai go for a docking?
faqs.a: Ocean-going bulk carriers and tankers normally dock at the large repair yards in Dalian, Qingdao, Zhoushan or the Yangtze delta. That is why measuring during a Yantai discharge is useful: the yard receives a steel renewal estimate before the ship arrives, and the same measurement locations can be used in dock so the class surveyor works from one consistent record.
